comment: Rules for `node scripts/test.js --changed`: the plans a change runs. Both kinds are applied to every changed file. A directory rule (`directoryRules`) looks the path up under test/plans/feat and names the deepest plan directory or plan file that mirrors it (modules/tensor/ops.cpp -> feat/modules/tensor, test/cases/compile/enum/x.cml -> feat/compile/enum.plan.toml); its `also` list adds plans that read every change under that directory beside the mirrored one, for a plan that reads a whole class of files rather than a directory of them (the front-end AST snapshot reads every `.cml`), and its entries take the rule entry forms above with the rule's `layer` as their default. A file rule (`rules`) then adds the plans outside that mirrored tree that the same change can also break (modules/tiles -> test/plans/gpu/tiles*, modules/onnx -> the exporter in feat/trans); the first matching file rule applies to a file, so keep them from specific to general. A rule entry is a path under test/plans, { "plan": path, "layer": true } or { "plan": path, "ownCases": true }: an ownCases plan is added only when the changed file is one of the `case` paths it names, so a slow plan cannot ride a shared directory into an edit it never reads ; a layered plan stays a named target but follows `--tier` like a directory, so the slow cases an ordinary change must not run (the PyTorch comparisons of autodiff and onnx) are filtered while the fast cases still run; `"layer": true` on the rule is the default for all its entries. A rule with "self": true selects the changed plan file itself (editing a plan runs that plan), except for the paths in "except": those select nothing, so a change there is refused instead of running perf, GC stress, progen or PyTorch. A non-plan file under test/plans (a golden, a fixture) selects the nearest directory that holds a plan, so editing a golden runs the plans it belongs to. A change no rule matches is refused (exit 2), naming every file that matched no rule: an empty selection must not become a plan expansion, and the fast layer is asked for deliberately with `--all` or with a plan name. It used to widen to the whole fast layer, and that widening is what this refusal replaces -- it ran the layer for a change that names no plan, and it left a record that no run could execute (a whole-layer selection keeps a count and a digest, not its rows), so the run refused the record it was handed as an empty selection; a change with no file in it selects no plan and runs none: `test/tools/run-tests.mjs#loadPlans` reads an empty target list as the whole plan tree, so an empty selection travels as `--selection-empty`, nothing starts and the run prints `changed: 0 target(s)`. That zero is also the only thing that names what the old fallback ran, and the old fallback did not run `the fast layer` either: measured 2026-11-05, 0 changed files started 336 plan files and 8879 test entries, where `npm run test` (the smoke and feat targets) is 330 plan files and 8858 -- the 6 extra are `test/plans/gpu`, so `widens to the whole fast layer` was a wrong name for a set larger than `npm run test`; a base branch, a changed-file list or this file that cannot be read is refused with exit 2 instead -- an unknown selection never becomes a layer. Every `--changed` reading names the base it was taken against, because a reading with no base is not a measurement: on 2026-11-05 the default base moved from 8e2159034 to 94cdfd1be (49 commits) inside one session, and the same tree then selected 36 plans against the default base and 4 against the pinned one -- the difference was other lanes' files, which is not an empty selection but a full one. `--changed --list` prints the selection without running it. The base branch is origin/develop; CAMEL_TEST_BASE overrides it. A tracked file that matches no rule is a hole, not a silent fallback: when a change also touches a file a rule matches, the unruled file contributes nothing. test/tools/selftest/run.mjs therefore fails on such a file unless it is on its allowlist, which names only the classes the project forbids (perf, GC stress, progen, PyTorch) or that no plan reads (vendored code, packaging, CI configuration). Deliberately not selectable: test/plans/perf/**, the GC-stress plans (feat/mm/gc*, gpu/tiles_regions) -- the project forbids those on a shared host, so a change there selects nothing and is refused, which is the report that says so, instead of wiring them in. The random-program plan (feat/opt/progen.plan.toml) is the one plan with a door and a lock: its own harness under test/tools/progen/ selects it, and nothing else does (a progen case or the plan file itself selects nothing), because a check that no change selects does not exist -- the classes of red that --tier fast hid were that same silence -- while 1,025 compiler runs must still not ride on an ordinary change of the corpus. The same self-test now checks the other direction too: every plan file under test/plans must be selected by at least one of the case paths it names, so a plan --changed can never reach cannot hide behind cases that select another plan; plans the policy keeps unselectable (perf, GC stress, the debug layer) and a sweep-only plan are the only exemptions, and progen is exempt there for the same reason it has a door: its cases are named by other plans. Update this file when a subsystem grows a plan of its own; see docs/test-plans.md, 'Selecting plans from a change', and its subsection 'The cases a change selects'. The rules here name plans; the run is a case list (`scripts/selection-cases.mjs`), so a case reached only through a plan-level reading is recorded as one: a changed `case` input selects the cases that name it and nothing else of that plan, and the layer applies per case -- a slow case does not run in the fast gate because its plan file was selected. `--changed --list` still prints this plan list, `--changed --list-cases` prints the case list with each case's cause, and a record kept under `test/selection/` holds the list a replay must reproduce -- a historical reading only: no gate step reads one, the record a gate runs on is computed on the spot for the run's own targets (`scripts/selection-cases.mjs --targets`), and a run that starts no test exits 2, because nothing was measured and a zero-row summary is the same three numbers a green run prints.

directoryRules.comment: The graph-space gradient case is a fast mm case that lives in the GC directory: the generic test/cases rule below resolves that directory to feat/mm/gc.plan.toml, the slow GC-stress plan, which does not run it. This exact path comes first and names no fall-through, so the file rule for the case selects feat/mm/graph_space instead.

The process-state cases are fast mm cases that live in the GC directory: the generic test/cases rule below resolves that directory to feat/mm/gc.plan.toml, the slow GC-stress plan, which runs neither of them. These exact paths come first and name no fall-through, so a change to either selects the feat/mm directory (layered, so the slow plans there still follow --tier).

The context-lifetime case is a fast mm case that lives in the GC directory as well: the generic test/cases rule below resolves that directory to feat/mm/gc.plan.toml, the slow GC-stress plan, which does not run it. This exact path comes first and names no fall-through, so the file rule for the case selects the plan that reads it.

The formatted-print case is a fast consistency program that happens to live under the cpp exec dump directory: the generic test/cases rule below resolves it to feat/trans/cpp.plan.toml, whose agree_with_fvm test compiles and runs C++ for up to ten minutes, and which does not run this case. This exact path comes first and falls through to the file rule that names print_formats.

The seed corpus of the progen finding cases (test/cases/opt/progen/findings): no plan directory mirrors it, and the generic test/cases rule below would resolve it to test/plans/feat/opt/progen.plan.toml -- the slow random-program check an ordinary change must never run in full. This rule comes first and names no fall-through, so the directory rule selects nothing here and the file rule for those cases names progen_simplify instead.
The cases whose own path starts with feat/ (test/cases/feat/mm, ...): the generic rule below would look for test/plans/feat/feat/mm. This narrower match comes first, so mm cases select feat/mm.

A test case: its directory is looked up under test/plans/feat (compile, linear, modules/tensor, modules/nn.plan.toml, tools/unicode -> tools, ...). Its `also` names the plan that reads every case of the tree: `feat/parse/frontend.plan.toml` hashes every `.cml` file of the repository into `test/plans/feat/parse/golden/ast_hashes.txt`, so a case that lands without being recorded there is a file that changed with nothing reading it. That hole is asymmetric, which is what makes it worth a rule: a change to the golden itself already selects the parse directory (a non-plan file under test/plans selects the plans that own it), so the only case nobody saw was the one nobody recorded. `layer` is true so `--tier fast` keeps the plan's fuzz test in the layer it belongs to; its snapshot test is 1.3 s, measured on the gate host.

The standard library is inside the module tree now (`lib/std/` holds the core's files and the passes, `lib/<module>/` a module), and a plan directory mirrors a module, not the library: this narrower match comes first, so a `lib/std/` change is read by the file rules only, the way a `src/passes/` change was before the layout move.

A module: lib/tensor selects feat/modules/tensor, lib/nn selects feat/modules/nn.plan.toml. A module with no plan of its own (python) falls through to the file rules. `modules/<module>/` before the layout move, which put a module's C++ under `modules/`; the directory is `lib/<module>/` now.
A tool: tools/lsp selects feat/tools/lsp.plan.toml; tools/format falls through to the file rules (feat/format).

rules.comment: The capture-order determinism reading's only case is the checker itself (scripts/check-capture-order.mjs): no plan directory mirrors a tool under scripts/, so the rule for scripts/ selects smoke and nothing would run the plan that reads the checker's output. This rule takes that one path out of the general rule (first match wins) and names the plan the checker feeds; the rest of scripts/ still selects smoke.

The three higher-order-clause readings keep their cases under test/cases/effects/ because what they observe is the footprint, while the plan sits in feat/compile because what it states is the operator's clause. The directory rule mirrors test/cases/effects/ to the feat/effects directory and the rule for that directory names feat/compile/effects_syntax, so neither reaches this plan; these three paths name it beside them.

The commit-tier reading's fixture lives with the other commit-check cases (test/cases/opt/commit_checks/), so the directory rule mirrors it to feat/opt/commit_checks.plan.toml, while the plan that reads it sits in feat/effects because the tier it asks about is the effect analysis's own commit check. This path names that plan beside the mirrored one.

The savepoint readings run over the rule pairs of rules_int.cml, a corpus file that feat/mm/writings.plan.toml also names: the directory rule selects the writings plan, so this path adds the savepoint plan beside it, and the half of the savepoint that takes back a whole segment runs when the corpus it reads changes.

The two programs the plan-refs plan reads, one from the counted-box table of the compile plans and one from the closure cases. The plan sits in test/plans/feat/tools, which no directory under test/plans/feat mirrors from a test/cases path, so the walk from test/cases reaches nothing here and this rule is the one the self-test asks for: every plan under test/plans must be selected by a case path it names. It comes before the general rules in this list because the first matching file rule applies to a file. Naming the two files adds this plan beside the one the directory rule selects (feat/compile, feat/consistency/values), and the plan is fast, so the rule carries no layer.

The plan-refs sweep: its case is the tool itself, so a change there selects the plan that runs it -- the same shape as the other tool cases in this list. The sweep is a plan of its own because its bound (1200000 ms, four times the CPU it spends starting one `camel` per case) would make any plan that also names it slow-cost, and a named plan file runs in full whatever `--tier` says.

The progen seed 23 program of the splice defect `a1723fbb9` fixed (test/cases/opt/inline_cycle): one program, one plan. It is a file rule and not a directory rule for the reason the adb67e081 rule below is one -- the directory rule for test/cases mirrors the segments below test/cases and would look for `test/plans/feat/opt/inline_cycle`, which is a plan file, so nothing would reach it. The plan is fast, so the rule carries no layer.

The reduced programs of the archiving result adb67e081 (test/cases/opt/adb67e081): the reductions of the finder's report, kept unedited. Two plans run them, and both are named here: `feat/opt/adb67e081` holds the programs whose defect is still open (work owed, so its `fail` count is the debt) and `feat/compile/fold_arms` holds `rc05_seed104`, the one this lane fixed. The rules come first in this list, before the general ones: the directory rule for test/cases below mirrors the segments below test/cases and would look for `test/plans/feat/opt/adb67e081`, which is a plan file, so nothing would reach it.

The writing-freedom comparator: its case is the tool itself, so a change there selects the two plans that run it -- `feat/compile/var` (the `var`-to-SSA pair) and `feat/compile/chain` (what a `sync` block's chain carries). Both are fast, so the rule carries no layer. The tool also has a --group spelling reading, quoted in examples/case-study/README.md and not gated: it compares the case study's program with three writings of it that change no meaning, and two of the three differ today, which is a defect to report and not a red to keep.
The corpus sweep tool: its case is the tool itself, so a change there selects the plan that runs it (a slow plan, so an ordinary change filters it out under --tier fast).

The probe cases of the canonical pack spelling (test/cases/probe): the programs that must still be refused and the accepted twins written with the canonical spelling. They are named as file rules because the three plans sit in test/plans/probe/, which no directory under test/plans/feat mirrors, and a directory rule cannot name them: its plan path is looked up by the segments below test/cases/probe/, and these cases are directly in that directory, so the lookup has no segment to add and answers with no plan. Naming the three files is the rule the self-test asks for -- every plan under test/plans must be selected by a case path it names.

The counted-box probes of test/probe/refleak (call_box.cml, fill_carries.cml; ad44fca33). They are named as a file rule for the reason the test/cases/probe rule above gives -- a directory rule cannot reach a plan under test/plans/probe from a case path -- and theirs is the one directory in the tree that no rule named at all, which the self-test reports as a tracked file `--changed` can never run. The plan is `tier = "debug"`, so it is exempt from the reachability check and is never run by `--changed`; what the rule buys is that the two programs are not an unowned file.
The `std::cml` round-trip comparator: its case is the tool itself, so a change there selects the plan that runs it. The plan is fast, so the rule carries no layer.

`camel inspect --copies` reads three programs, and none of them is under test/plans/feat: the two append loops (test/cases/consistency/new_values/rebinding_loop.cml) and two training steps (test/cases/modules/optim/training.cml, examples/case-study/train.cml). Its plan sits in test/plans/feat/tools/, which no mirrored directory reaches from those cases, so the case directories are named here. The self-test asks every plan under test/plans to be selected by a case path it names, and the commit that added the plan named none, so `--changed` could never run it. The plan is fast, so the rule carries no layer.

The plan-normaliser guard: its case is the tool itself, so a change there selects the plan that runs it. Its two fixture trees under test/tools/selftest/plan-normalizers are read by that plan as well, which is why the selftest rule below names it too. The plan is fast, so the rule carries no layer.

The plan-field guard and the count it ratchets against: both are read by `feat/tools/plan_fields` alone, and the baseline is a tracked file, so naming it here is also what keeps it out of the rule-less class the self-test refuses. The plan is fast, so the rule carries no layer.

The parse-check harness, the selftest fixtures and the load-class guard: a change here runs smoke, the runner plan, the load-class plan (its cases are the selftest fixtures) and the front-end plan (layered so its slow fuzz test is filtered under --tier fast).

The runner itself and the self-test: the plans that exercise the runner and the smoke set. `feat/tools/plan_fields` is here too, because its second entry reads `test/tools/run-tests.mjs` itself: a field that moves out of a kind-gated block, or a fourth gated kind, is a red there, and a change to the runner is the only thing that can cause it. `feat/tools/selfchecks` starts the two self-tests that read the selection engine and the runner, so a change to either is the change they exist to be run on; it follows `--tier`, because its one slow entry copies `test/tools` and starts the engine several times.
The diagnostic-form checker reads the tools that parse a diagnostic out of a run: a change to it, or to a tool it names, re-runs the plan that holds its reading.

The self-tests of the derivative tables (`vjp_api.*` of feat/compile/transforms): each of the four is a `case` of that plan. `check-vjp-parity.mjs` runs `scripts/vjp-parity.mjs` on a copy of the rulesets and of the exemption list, `check-vjp-ruleset.mjs` the two ruleset imports, and the two refusal checks the tables the refusals are written in. A change to any of them must run the plan whose readings they are; smoke and the runner plan are the two the general `test/tools/` rule reached before, and they stay, because the first matching rule replaces it for a file.

The pass-parameter guards: `feat/opt/pass_params` runs `check-pass-declarations.mjs` as a case and the five readings of `check-doc-pass-forms.mjs`. A change to either guard is the check that plan holds, and the general `test/tools/` rule reaches neither it nor the two plans named after it.

The stdlib-registry guards: `check-env-switches.mjs` and `check-no-algo.mjs` are two of the fourteen cases of `feat/modules/stdlib_registry` (`registry.no_env_switches`, `registry.algo_module_gone`), which is the plan that would report a regression in either.

The tooling's own tests, three rules for three families: a `*.test.mjs` beside the tool it tests is read by `feat/tools/selfchecks` and by nothing else, so an edit to the test or to the tool under it must run that plan -- otherwise the file that checks the tool is green only because nothing reads it. Each rule re-lists the plans its family reached before (`smoke` from the `scripts/` rule, `smoke` and the runner plan from the general `test/tools/` rule, `feat/docs_links` from the `internal/tools/` rule), because the first matching rule replaces the general one for a file. The `*.test.ps1` files are the class these rules leave out: a plan cannot start one (the build host has no pwsh, and the runner resolves a tool that is neither `node` nor `python` inside the install), and `scripts/plan-inventory.mjs#selfCheckProblems` names every one of them with that reason.

The next two families of the rule above: the checks beside the tools of `internal/tools` and of `scripts`, and the tools they cover. `feat/tools/selfchecks` starts them; `feat/docs_links` is what the `internal/tools/` rule reached before (its citation and conflict-marker walks read those `.ps1` and `.mjs` files), and `smoke` is what the `scripts/` rule reached before.

The checks of the `scripts/` tools: the merge gate's readers, the case-selection record and the two counters. No plan but the one that starts them reads either half of a pair, so a change to a test or to the tool it tests runs `feat/tools/selfchecks`; `smoke` stays because the `scripts/` rule reached it before.

The DAP race harness that `feat/tools/load_class` drives under load. It lives in test/tools/debugger but is not one of the debugger's DAP cases: the debugger plan reached it only because the directory rule below covers the directory, and that plan is kept here so the change runs no less than it did.
The argument-domain table of the command line: `cli.arg_domains_match_the_cli` runs it and holds it against what the binary refuses, so a change to the table must run feat/tools/cli.
The import-cost audit: the `case` of feat/modules/import_cost, which starts it over the module tree.
The collection fuzzer: `feat/compile/collections` runs it as its quick case. Its only other reader is the GC-stress plan, which an ordinary change must not run, so that plan is not named here.

The C++ execution harness `run.py`: `feat/trans/cpp` runs it for seven of its cases and the keyed-random comparison of `feat/modules/random` drives it too, so both plans are named. The general `test/tools/` rule would send it to smoke, which compiles no C++ at all.
The repeated-run half of the C++ harness: `feat/trans/cpp` runs it as a case of its own, and no other plan does.
The capacity-scale driver: the thirteen readings of `feat/mm/capacity` are runs of it.
The debugger harness (the DAP race harness): the plan whose slow DAP cases it drives. A harness change is not a plan change, but this is the plan that would catch a regression in it.
The language-server test client.

The random-program harness (test/tools/progen). Its case is the program generator itself, so the plan that runs it is the smallest honest check of a change there, and this is the only path that selects it: editing a progen case or the progen plan file still selects nothing, because 1,025 compiler runs must not ride on an ordinary change of that corpus. This rule comes before the general test/tools rule below, which it replaces for these files. It carries no `layer`, so the plan is named and runs in full: the batch (`progen_check`, milestone) and the single seed it broke last (`progen_seed_4`, fast) are both readings a harness change has to produce, because a plan that is selected and then filtered down to one entry is the same silence in a new place. Cost, measured on the gate host at -Jobs 8: 1,025 cells, 27 s of wall (100 s of CPU), the reading progen_check records.

The same-graph comparator (test/tools/same_graph.py): its case is the tool itself, so a change there selects the plan that runs it -- `feat/trans/same_graph` -- and that plan is fast, so the rule carries no layer. This rule comes before the general test/tools rule below, which it replaces for this file. The plan is named and runs in full because the whole of what the tool decides is which readings a pair of writings gets: the verdict on the criterion's own pair, the pair of pure writings that says the canonical form is order-independent at all, and the two counterexamples that keep a `true` from being vacuous.

The second-pass CPU reading (`test/tools/opt-cost/second_pass.mjs`) and the plan that owns it. Both of the plan's cases live in the tool's own directory and nowhere under test/cases, so the general test/tools rule below selects the runner plan and not this one: measured 2026-11-22, `test/plans/feat/opt/opt_second_pass.plan.toml` was selected by no case path at all and the runner self-test reported it as a plan `--changed` can never run. The directory holds that tool and nothing else, so the rule names the directory and the plan runs in full: its two entries are 120 s each and both read the same helper, so an edit to part of it is an edit to the reading. This rule comes before the general test/tools rule, which it replaces for this path.

The other test harnesses (cppexec, parsecheck, jitcov, gcbench, ...): no plan tests a harness directly, and naming the plan that invokes one would mean naming most of feat/. The smallest honest check is smoke plus the runner plan, which is what a harness change can break first. The specific debugger and LSP clients above are narrower because their plans own them.

The gate entry and the helpers beside it (internal/tools): the tools that move a tree to the build host, build and run plans there, the local build and test helpers, the watcher, the settings loader, the example settings file and their README. No plan exercises them -- they are the harness that runs the plans, they run on the workstation under PowerShell, and the build host has no pwsh -- so there is no behavioural plan to name, and naming smoke here would be the shape of a guard that guards nothing. They are still read, though, which is why this is a rule and not a rule-less class: scripts/conflict-markers.mjs walks every tracked file whose extension it knows (.md, .ps1 and .json are all in that set) and scripts/check-doc-links.mjs --citations reads .ps1 and .md from the repository root, and both are tests of feat/docs_links. Measured on 2026-11-04: one hunk head appended to internal/tools/watch-fsh-dev.ps1 is reported as internal/tools/watch-fsh-dev.ps1:71, and one stale `*.md` citation in a .ps1 or a .md under internal/tools is reported by name. So `--changed` on a gate-script edit runs feat/docs_links, and a merge left unfinished or a citation that stops resolving in one of these files goes red there. That is the whole of what the plan sees: it does not verify what the gate does. A file added here that neither walker reads is a new hole, and must not be read as covered because this rule exists.

The backlog (internal/backlog.md): a row there is a statement about work, and the file is a page like any other -- `scripts/check-doc-links.mjs --citations` reads every `*.md` path the tree cites, and `scripts/conflict-markers.mjs` walks it with the same set of extensions. It had no rule, so a change that touched only backlog rows and plan pages matched nothing at all: `--changed` widened to the whole fast layer while the merge side read 'this merge selects no plan'. That is a documentation merge which cannot be measured and therefore cannot be advanced -- the gap is that it cannot be measured, not that the selection is slow. feat/docs_links is the plan that reads it.

The plan pages (internal/plans/): the pages a dispatch is written on, and the reports beside them. They are read the same way the backlog is -- `--citations` resolves every `*.md` path mentioned in them, and the conflict-marker walk covers them -- so a change to a page is a documentation change with a plan that reads it, not a change no rule matches. Widening to the fast layer instead would run the widest row of the covering table for a page whose only reader is a link check.

The public headers mirror the blocks: a header a pass or the runtime includes is as wide as the source file that includes it. These rules mirror the source rules below, so a header change selects the same plans as the implementation it declares. They come first because the layout map (`docs/design/architecture/layout-map.cn.md`, table B) put each block's headers inside the block's own directory (`kernel/include/`, `parse/include/`, `compile/include/`, `lib/<module>/include/`): a rule is matched by prefix, so a header rule placed after its block's source rule would never fire. The front end is the block this sentence is the exception to: it is one rule for the whole of `src/parse/`, header and source, because a change to the grammar is a change to every tool that reads the syntax, and that list belongs in one place. It also covers the block's `CMakeLists.txt`, which no rule named before -- a change there widened to the whole fast layer. The tools, and what each reads: `feat/tools/lsp` (the syntax index every definition, hover, highlight and reference answer comes from), `feat/format` (camel-fmt prints the tree the parser built, and the corpus it is checked on is written in the grammar under test), `feat/trans/cml` (`std::cml` prints a program to text and that text is compiled back), `feat/tools/debugger` (a breakpoint and a step are placed by source position), `feat/modules/stdlib_registry` (`scripts/stdlib-reference.mjs --verify-docs` compiles the `@example` of every declaration, and `--verify-doc` regenerates the reference page from the sources) and `feat/trans/source_spelling` (the samples `std::cml`, camel-format and progen write are compiled back). The ruling this rule is: on 2026-11-23 `9622bd21c9` rewrote a lambda as `func (x) { x * x }` and its gate ran `feat/parse` and `feat/compile` only; both were green, while the syntax index kept walking a lambda body only when it saw a `=>` and every name inside a lambda body lost its reference -- definition, hover, highlight and references answered nothing, on every lambda in the tree, and no plan was asked.
The compiler and graph headers. `compile/include/camel/compile/gir/draft_graph_builder.h` is the only door from a handle to the builder that owns it, so the witness of that identity runs with it.
The pass API headers: the translation, optimization and scheduler passes. The move distributed them over the block that owns each pass, so the rule names each block's `camel/passes/` directory.

The core value/type headers and the runtime headers. The array type's dimensions live here, so its self-test runs too. The ledger's `files`/`references` count is partly a header count (`kernel/include/camel/runtime/draft.h`, `draft_session.h`, ...), so this rule names the ledger plan for the same reason the core one does. `kernel/include/camel/runtime/node_ref.h` is where a handle's identity is written down -- the address and the epoch -- so the witness of it runs here too.
The executor and entry-argument headers.
Any other public header (init, utils, services, the standalone bridge): the compiler, the translator and the runtime, which is the smallest set every consumer of the blocks' include roots shares.

FastVM and the other schedulers. The scheduler is also where a collection can be asked for, which makes this the file class that decides when an object dies: `feat/opt/defun.plan.toml` reads programs whose values are function values and closures, `feat/compile/ref.plan.toml` reads the box counts a run takes and releases, and `feat/mm/graph_space.plan.toml` is the graph-space gradient case that runs a real collection. On 2026-11-15 a collection added after the entry graph returned in `nodevm.cpp` was selected by feat/linear, feat/para, feat/trans and smoke, none of which runs a program that keeps a function value alive; it passed all of them and broke eight `defun` program runs (`killed by a signal: 8`) plus one assertion, all red on a pushed HEAD until the change was reverted. The judgement this rule records is not the three plans but the class: any file that can change what may be treated as a root takes every plan that depends on when an object dies with it.

The optimization passes and the rewrite rule library they run: the opt plans, the pass dumps that print their effect, the rewrite-rule plan, and feat/compile for the module registration and operator declarations a rewrite-module change can break. stdlib/rules.cml is the data these passes run, so it selects the same set. `feat/opt` is a directory target, so `--tier fast` keeps its fast plans and filters the slow progen plan (progen is never selected by a rule). The rule library's own SMT check is selected here too: it reads stdlib/rules.cml, so a rule that stops holding under its licence is reported by the change that edited it.

The rule verifier's translation layer (`src/stdlib/verify/translate.cpp`, `translate.h`): it is not a module -- it registers no operator, and `src/stdlib/verify/CMakeLists.txt` compiles it into modules/rewrite -- so it selects what a change to the module selects, plus `rules_differential` (the differential check reads the translation of a rule into witnesses). The rule is here and not left to the directory rule because no plan mirrors the directory: `src/stdlib/verify/` has no plan file, so the mirror looked for `test/plans/feat/modules/verify`, which held only the three verifier scripts below, and `--changed` refused the run with exit 2 -- a refusal that reads as an unreadable tree rather than as a selection. Measured on 2026-11-23: `--list` exited 2 with `test/plans/feat/modules/verify holds no *.plan.toml`, and exits 0 selecting these seven plans now that the directory holds no plan-less sibling.

The three scripts that judge a rule library (`test/cases/modules/rules/verify/*.mjs`): `feat/modules/rules.plan.toml` runs `check_covers_every_rule.mjs` as its verify script and `check_covers_every_rule_rejects_refuted.mjs` as a case, and `feat/modules/rules_differential.plan.toml` runs `differential_equivalence.mjs`. The mirror alone is not enough: a file under `test/cases/modules/rules/verify/` resolves to `rules.plan.toml` (the plan file its grandparent directory names), which runs neither of the other two. `rules_proofs` is named by the rule above and not here, because it runs no case of this class and a named plan file runs in full (the self-test refuses a costly plan named for a case it does not run).
The profiler pass: its own plan runs without a CUDA device (the host fallback), so it is safe from an ordinary change.
The other translation passes: the graph printers, the C++ emitter, the JSON dump.
The test-only passes (test::facts, test::regions, test::rules, ...): the plans that name them in their arguments.
Any other pass, including the shared pass machinery.

GCT/GIR construction, encoding and the graph printer. `src/compile/gir/builder_support.h` is where a node handle is turned back into the draft it names and where that identity is checked, so the witness of the identity (`feat/runtime/draft_node_owner.plan.toml`) runs with it.

Values, types, the collector and the runtime shell. The array type's dimensions live here, so its self-test runs too. The direct-connection ledger of graph-store step 2 b is checked here as well: its three numbers count the references to `GraphDraft`, and `src/runtime/` is where both the storage and the transaction live, so this is the directory a commit can add a direct connection from. The plan is fast and cheap (one `git grep` pass), so it rides along rather than waiting for its own gate. The witness of a node handle's identity rides along for the same reason: the epoch a handle names its draft by is minted in `src/runtime/draft.cpp`.
Execution, entry arguments and the standalone bridge.

The rest of src/: the built-in operators and their semantic tables (src/builtin) are the core every module plan runs on, so feat/modules is included; the services, profiler helpers and utilities are reached through the compiler and the runtime. The specific rules above stay narrower.

Tiles, the module: the CPU plan, the three GPU plans (all slow, so they are named as plan files and run in full even under --tier fast), the profile and reading plans, and the DDPM plan whose training cases are written against tiles. A module change can invalidate every consumer, and the GPU plans are what no directory rule could reach before.

A tiles case: the CPU plan is the directory mirror, and the DDPM, profile and reading plans read some of these cases. The three GPU plans are slow (88 tests) and are added only for the cases they name (`ownCases`): a case edit cannot invalidate a GPU plan that does not run it, which is what kept a one-case edit running a whole GPU plan in full. The GPU plan that shares a case with a fast plan is recorded in `slowCaseOwners`.

The ONNX exporter. `layer` is true because the plan's four slow cases are ONNX Runtime and PyTorch comparisons: under --tier fast the fast exporter tests run and those are filtered; --tier all runs them. `feat/trans` holds the dumps that print the exported graph. `onnx_with_forms` pins the three call forms of `export_model`'s `with` list (only `out`; `out` with `target`; `out` with `dynamic_axes`), one case under `test/cases/modules/onnx/with_forms/` each.
Neural-network operators: the nn plan and the plans that train with them.
Automatic differentiation. `layer` is true because five slow cases compare gradients against PyTorch: --tier fast runs the fast autodiff cases and filters those.

The showcase's first-step gradient: `feat/showcase_s2.plan.toml` reads one case under test/cases/compile/transforms/, which the directory rules mirror to feat/compile/transforms.plan.toml, and it sits beside the feat/ plans rather than in that mirrored directory, so no case path selected it and `--changed` could never reach it. `ownCases` keeps the rule from riding every edit in that directory into a plan that reads one program. This and the `feat/compile/rules_angle_args.plan.toml` entry above are the author's 2026-11-03 ruling on the red self-test carried out: the two names the self-test reports are a rule missing from this file, and the runner has nothing to do with it.

Tensor operators and shapes: the tensor plans, the index/operator semantics plans, the thread budget (the pool and the library GEMM share one number), the numeric licence that the library path is allowed under, and autodiff (layered, for the same PyTorch reason), because a shape or operator change shows up in gradients.

Keyed random: the random plan, whose slow std::cpp comparison follows --tier (`layer`) so a change to a case does not run it in full, the reference plan that runs the Philox cases, and the registry that lists them.
Graph values and passes, and the rewrite rules built on them.
Checkpoint trees.

The declaration modules with no plan of their own: their cases live under test/cases/modules/std, which feat/modules/std.plan.toml runs, and their signatures are checked by the registry plan.

That is exactly feat/modules/stdlib_registry, so this rule is narrower than the declaration-body rule below and comes first (`lib/<module>/signatures/` is inside a module directory the catch-all below would otherwise take).

The list is every declaration that has no module rule of its own: it is a list and not a prefix because the move put each declaration inside its module's directory, and a module added later without a rule of its own is a tracked file no rule names -- which the runner self-test reports by name.
The std facade over the modules: the module plan that exercises it, the compile checks of its imports, and the registry that lists its operators.

Any other module (a module's C++ that no rule above names). `lib/` is the module tree after the layout move, `modules/` before it. A directory target, so --tier fast filters the slow cases; a module that grows a specific rule above stops using this one.
The language server, debugger, formatter and command-line tools.

Nothing else reads these pages: no plan runs a backlog row, and smoke is a compiler layer, so it is not named here (unlike the reader-facing docs rule above, which names it because that rule is written for the report gate).

The README and the findings index are documentation of the manual progen tool and are on the self-test's rule-less allowlist.

The reduced seed 8 program of the branch-arm refusal (`std::opt` on the progen batch, `JOIN 113 reads GATE 217` before the reduction): it lives in the progen corpus, whose directory rule above selects nothing, so the fast plan that runs it is named here. Without this rule the plan would be one `--changed` can never reach, which is the hole the same case path is meant to close.

The checkpoint fixtures of the nn plan: `checkpoint_fixture.mjs` (the committed native checkpoint loads) and `checkpoint_verify.mjs` (the state round-trips) are two cases of `feat/modules/checkpoints`. Their directory resolves to feat/modules/nn.plan.toml, which runs neither, so the plan that holds their readings had to be named.

The branch-shape comparison of `feat/opt/equal_branch`: the same directory as the rule above, and the same reason -- the plan that runs it is not the one the directory mirrors. It is a separate rule and not a second path in that one, because an edit to either comparison must not select the other plan.

The three pass-declaration cases: they live under test/cases/tools/cli, whose directory resolves to feat/tools/cli.plan.toml, and their own plan is `feat/opt/pass_params` (the declaration of a pass parameter, its effect, and the same machinery as a call).

A plan file selects itself: editing the tests of one plan runs that plan. A non-plan file under test/plans (a golden, a fixture) selects the nearest directory that holds a plan, so editing a golden runs the plans it belongs to. The except list keeps the plans the project forbids from an ordinary change out of that: a perf, GC-stress or progen plan edit falls back to the fast layer (name the plan file to run it deliberately).

slowCaseOwners.comment: Slow plans whose cases live in a directory a fast plan also uses. `ownCases` already keeps such a plan off the cases it does not run; this list records the cases it does run that a fast plan also runs, where the slow plan is therefore not the only owner of the changed path. The reason says why the slow plan must still run. The self-test derives the facts: it requires every entry to be a slow-cost plan (tier slow, a slow test, or a timeout of five minutes or more) that names at least one case a fast plan also names, so an entry that excuses nothing fails.

entries.why: Its GPU tests share resident.cml with the fast screens plan: a case that a fast and a slow plan both exercise can break only on one of them, so the case edit must run both. The plan stays slow because it needs a CUDA device and its 83 tests take minutes.
